## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Background

Cross country and track are the two main running sports that comprise most of the calendar year for competitive runners, from high school through college and even the professional level. In cross country, runners trek through long distance races over sprawling courses. In track, there is a wide variety of races runners may participate in, from short sprints to many laps around the oval. Cross country occurs during the fall, while track occurs during the winter, spring, and into summer. Unlike sports such as basketball or volleyball, which are most often conducted in controlled environments, the sport of running is highly variable. The courses on which races are held can be very different from each other even if the distances are largely the same. Performance can be highly impacted by weather, conditions, location, time of the season, race stakes, and many other factors. 
  
  This project seeks to examine these outside factors and their influence on U.S. collegiate club running performance in particular. At major institutions, the sport of running generally falls within two levels: the varsity scholarship level and the club running level. The National Intercollegiate Running Club Association (NIRCA) is the main governing body of collegiate running clubs across the United States. These running clubs exist outside the NCAA and varsity scholarship athletics, allowing all runners the opportunity to compete and enjoy the sport. Member athletes can compete in club-sponsored races hosted across the country. They may also participate in regional races where they can compete against NCAA athletes. NIRCA encompasses both club cross country and club track, covering a wide range of races and distances.

### 1.2 Motivation

The tracking of statistics related to running performance is relatively new; whereas statistics have always been at the forefront of athlete analysis in major sports such as football and basketball, it is relatively recently that race data has begun to be seen as a useful tool for understanding the variability that comes with the sport. Online tools such as *Athletic.net* and *TFFRS* were founded in the 2000s to be able to host race results. However, these sites tend to only contain very basic results data: runner name, year, team, placement, overall time, and sometimes the average pace per mile. Thus, it can be hard to put into context the performances of the athletes.

  There exist some papers written within the past few years years that examine influencing factors on race-day performance, mainly focused on weather parameters. Many of these papers focus on the marathon distance; for instance, Knechtle et. al (2019) specifically looked at years of Boston Marathon results to determine the relationship between weather conditions, sex, country of origin, and running performance. Another paper by Mantzios et al. (2022) looked into the implications of temperature, humidity, and wind speed on performance in endurance running events across the globe, finding that heat has a particularly strong impact on reducing peak running abilities. While these papers determine some conditions that considerably impact running performance, they are mostly limited to very long distances (10K, marathons, etc.) and tend to focus mostly on weather variables only. Furthermore, these athletes tend to be professional runners and older. It should be noted that marathon athletes and races make up only a fraction of the sport.

  Researchers at Notre Dame, the founders of the dataset we seek to work with, wrote one of the first papers to use a publicly available running dataset that expands scope beyond the marathon. Their paper looks to provide an evidence-based framework on ideal race scheduling at the collegiate level based on athlete improvement trends throughout racing season (Karr, Fryer, et al., 2026). However, their research questions center around the athletes themselves, focusing on their improvement within a season and across multiple seasons. With our project, we hope to specifically examine the outside factors available in this dataset that contribute to the race environment and ultimately influence athlete performance, from weather and topography to race stakes. Our research will fill in some gaps identified earlier, including looking at a wider range of race types and focusing attention on a range of collegiate athletes rather than only professional runners and road racers. In this way, our findings become more relevant to a wider group of runners; it can provide valuable information on which "uncontrollable" factors impact race day the most so athletes can be best prepared to handle them.
    
### 1.3 Research Questions 
  
The following research questions center around factors that surround races, going beyond variables inherent to the athletes themselves:
  
- Do certain weather conditions impact performances across various race lengths differently? If so, how, and to what extent?
- How might race locations, especially in terms of altitude, climate, and topography, affect athlete performance?
- Do the stakes of the race (regional, national, NIRCA-only, NCAA-hosted, early season/late season, etc.) push athletes to perform better?  



## 2. Data

### 2.1 Data Background and Sources
  
This investigation analyzes the public National Running Club Database (NRCD), archived on Zenodo (Karr, Darden, et al., 2026). The NRCD was originally founded and built by researchers at the University of Notre Dame, led by creator Jonathan A. Karr Jr., to give collegiate club runners the shared results infrastructure that NCAA Division I programs have historically enjoyed. Prior to the NRCD, public running data was heavily restricted, scattered across private spreadsheets or PDFs, or limited to small-scale studies without public downloadable datasets. The reliability and trustworthiness of the NRCD stem from its unique, moderated data collection pipeline. Unlike unverified web scrapes, results are submitted by club athletes and administrators, and then carefully reviewed and approved by moderators before entering the official corpus.


### 2.2 General Data Description

This project uses the `joined.csv` file from the NRCD dataset. The dataset is very large containing 180,767 rows (observations) and 70 columns (variables). The variables in this dataset encompass a wide variety of race factors, ranging from athlete details (gender, grade, team_name, result_time) to race and environment details (meet_city, altitude, event_type, and 21 variables that relate to aspects of the weather, such as wind and temperature). ID variables (result_id, meet_id, sport_id) give each result and event type a unique numerical identifier, while binary variables (regionals, nationals) identify the stakes of the race. From environmental factors to standardized times and venue data across many entries, this sampling of variables gives a glimpse into the breadth of the dataset.  
  
This dataset is useful to answer our research questions because it provides us with a wealth of information that goes beyond the race itself, from weather conditions to location and meet details that our research questions will require. The specificity of variables within this set will help us quantify trends and narrow down exactly which factors impact running performance. While traditional public tools like *Athletic.net*, *TFRRS*, and NCAA sites generally only report on basic variables such as runner names, teams, placements, and overall times without contextual depth, our data set has 70 different variables to consider. It includes crucial metrics ranging from exact runner start and end times to situational parameters like altitude, event types, temperatures, humidity, and wind. Because of this depth, we have the ability to look deeper into what affects performance.  


## 3. Exploratory Data Analysis

### 3.1 Data Cleaning

The initial dataset contained results from the main collegiate running sports of cross country and track, Because this study focuses specifically on individual running performance, the initial phase of our data cleaning process centered around excluding entries for non-running track events and relay results from the analytical dataset. Standard naming conventions of running events, typically a numerical distance followed by a unit of length such as "5000m", were used to distinguish eligible running events from other athletic competitions. Furthermore, the last 11 columns were excluded from our analysis since they do not pertain to our stated goals. This leaves 59 available variables and around 165000 observations.

```{r}
run = read.csv('joined.csv')
dim(run)
```

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidytext)

# First, exclude all non-running events and relay races

trues = str_detect(run$event_name, '(\\d{2,5}m)|(Marathon)|(Mile)') &
        !str_detect(run$event_name, 'x')

only_run = run[trues, ]
dim(only_run)
  
```

```{r}
# Next, grab only columns that could pertain to research questions
# Exclude relay columns, racewalk columns

only_run = only_run %>% select(1:59)
dim(only_run)
```

#### Duplication Cleanup

This dataset includes over 21000 rows where the result_ids are duplicated. As a part of the cleaning process, we investigated these rows to determine which ones were exact duplicates. There were 1,653 exact duplicate entries, which left us with 20297 rows that had duplicate `result_id` numbers but were not exact duplicate rows. Initial findings saw that these rows tend to have slight negligible differences in weather measurements, potentially due to multiple weather recordings at a race or track meet. Otherwise, these rows seemed to contain the same result for a unique athlete. 

To prove this finding, we utilized a pipeline that filtered to duplicate result ID's; summarizing on the ID variables `athlete_id` and `meet_id` helped determine if each duplicated result id had a one-to-one relationship with the athlete and meet. We also used `result_time` to solidify whether these rows contained the same exact result, since the times more strongly identify a unique performance down to the second. Finally, using `count` returned a one-row result indicating that all duplicated result ID's correspond with one unique athlete and result. Thus, we concluded there is a high likelihood these are redundant. We made the decision to accept the first recorded entry for each duplicated result ID, since weather parameters are unlikely to change dramatically in the relatively small amount of race time.

After filtering out duplicate entries, we are left with ~130000 observations.

```{r}
# Filter out exact duplicate entries

only_run = only_run %>% distinct()
dim(only_run)
```

```{r}
# Are remaining duplicate result_ids nearly the same?

dp = only_run %>%
  group_by(result_id) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    athletes = n_distinct(athlete_id),
    times = n_distinct(result_time),
    meets = n_distinct(meet_id),
  ) %>%
  count(athletes, times, meets)

dp

only_run = only_run %>% distinct(result_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
dim(only_run)
```

#### Missing Data Cleanup

For key variables, which include ID variables, location, race classification, race distance, gender, and result time, there is rarely missing data. However, weather and climate variables experience more missing data; according to Karr, Fryer, et al. (2026), "meets from August 2023 onward carry comprehensive course distance, elevation gain and loss, weather at race time, and track venue metadata." Data on meets prior to this have much more limited information on weather, and indoor track meets will, of course, not have weather data present. It is not simple to fill in this missing metadata since each meet and athlete is unique while weather is highly variable; it is also not ideal to just simply omit rows without this metadata as most entries without it are still valid and valuable to other analysis. Thus, it was decided that a boolean variable `weather_true` would be created to help filter on entries that include data; this way, the original data is preserved, while weather analysis can simply filter on this new variable.

The new variable `weather_true` was built based on the `temperature` variable, which is always present for every entry that contains weather data.

```{r}
# Show that temperature is always present for every entry with weather
# Should return zero rows since it is always present with other weather
only_run %>%
  filter(is.na(temperature) & !is.na(humidity)) %>%
  nrow()

# Create new variable to filter on
only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(weather_true = !is.na(temperature))
```

There is a general set of weather variables always present together, including ones like `temperature`, `dew_point`, and `humidity`. Some niche weather variables simply don't have enough data to justify including them in analysis. **Renee please finish this part, try to justify why you might not use particular columns by showing like percent missing or whatever works. And then any other weather variables you want to clean.** 

#### Miscellaneous Variable Cleanup

The variable `event_type` could be very valuable for the stated goal of RQ3 in terms of the stakes of the race (prelims, finals, championship, etc.), but there are many missing values. Furthermore, when investigating unique event types, there are some typos and slight differences between names that cause the same event type to be essentially duplicated. To clean this variable, we first standardized existing names. Typos were addressed, and synonyms were combined into a single event type; "A" and "B" races were combined regardless of gender since a gender variable already exists to differentiate between them. 

We were also able to fill in some missing values based on existing knowledge of the sport. For instance, all cross country races are one-time races (no prelims and finals), and it is reasonable to assume that the races not marked as a "regional" or "national" are simply regular season races. Thus, these entries were filled in as "Regular Season". Track entries with missing event types were left alone as it is much more difficult to simply guess those event types. Again, it is not in the best interest of our analysis to omit entries with missing values for this variable as they still contain valid, important information elsewhere.

```{r}
# Investigate messy event_type variable
# only_run %>%
  # count(event_type, sort = TRUE)

# unique(only_run$event_type)

only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(event_type = case_when(
    event_type %in% c("Final", "Finals", "FInals") ~ "Finals",
    event_type %in% c("Prelims", "Pelims", "1st Round",
                      "Round 1", "Qualifying") ~ "Prelims",
    event_type %in% c("Invite", "Invitational") ~ "Invitational",
    event_type %in% c("FR/SO", "Freshman/Sophmore",
                      "Freshman/Sophomore") ~ "Freshman/Sophomore",
    event_type %in% c("JR/SR/GRAD", "Junior/Senior/Grad") ~ "Junior/Senior/Grad",
    event_type %in% c("A Race", "Men A", "Women A",
                      "Men's A Race", "Women's A Race") ~ "A Race",
    event_type %in% c("B Race", "Men B", "Women B",
                      "Men's B Race", "Women's B Race") ~ "B Race",
    event_type == "" & regionals == FALSE & nationals == FALSE &
  sport_name == "Cross Country" ~ "Regular Season",
    TRUE ~ event_type
  ))

length(unique(only_run$event_type))
# only_run %>%
  # count(event_type, sort = TRUE)
```

For the variable `event_name`, there are a number of non-standard running events that have minimal numbers of entries. For instance, 7000m is a non-standard cross country distance with only two recorded entries in the dataset. It was determined after reviewing a summary of counts by event and sport name that events with 100 or less observations tended to be niche events. For cleanest data and to compare performances across standardized times, we filtered out these non-standard, low-frequency niche race events (defined as event classifications with fewer than 200 total observations dataset-wide). Removing these single-instance anomalies will prevent any skewed performance metrics without meaningfully altering the overall dataset size.

Prior to filtering, the dataset contained 37 unique race events. After removing non-standard and niche events with fewer than 100 total entries, 24 unique event types remain, with only a reduction in observations by just over 1000 entries.

```{r}
# Investigate niche events
event_summary = only_run %>%
  count(sport_name, event_name, name = "count") %>%
  arrange(count) %>%
  filter(count < 200) %>%
  arrange(count)

event_summary
```


### 3.2 Data Summary

"Race Stakes" variables, are variables that define the context of a meet. This could be classifying the race as club-only (`nirca_only`), regionals (`regionals`), or nationals (`nationals`), which are typically end-of-season championship meets. Furthermore, the variable `event_type` breaks it down with even further context, especially for track events when there may be preliminary and final rounds. The variables `nirca_only`, `regionals`, and `nationals` are each logical/Boolean vectors denoting the race classification.

Table _ below displays the counts of entries under each classification and the total percent that each make up in the larger dataset. This table is designed to show the overlap that occurs between classifications - for instance, all regional and national meets are also classified as NIRCA (club) running meets only. There are some NIRCA-only regular season meets as well as meets that fall outside the NIRCA designation (could be NCAA, road races, etc.)

```{r}
stakes_summary = only_run %>%
  count(regionals, nationals, nirca_only, name = "count") %>%
  mutate(percentage = count / sum(count) * 100)

kable(
  stakes_summary,
  caption = "Table _: Number of Entries in Each Race Stakes Classification"
)
```

Table _ above reveals there are four combinations of race classification: NIRCA-only (regular season), NIRCA regionals, NIRCA nationals, and non-NIRCA (races not governed by NIRCA, which can include NCAA and other road races). To best visualize this, Figure _ below shows the proportion of race entries categorized by each meet stakes combination. Regular season NIRCA competitions account for the largest share of entries, followed by NIRCA Nationals, non-NIRCA open meets, and NIRCA Regionals.

```{r}
stakes_summary_class = stakes_summary %>%
  mutate(
    stake_category = case_when(
      !regionals & !nationals & !nirca_only ~ "Open / Non-NIRCA Meets",
      !regionals & !nationals & nirca_only  ~ "NIRCA Regular Season",
      !regionals & nationals & nirca_only   ~ "NIRCA Nationals",
      regionals & !nationals & nirca_only   ~ "NIRCA Regionals",
    )
  )

ggplot(stakes_summary_class, aes(x = reorder(stake_category, percentage), y = percentage)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure _: Distribution of Race Data by Stakes Classification",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Percentage of Total Entries (%)"
  )
```

With the "Sports and Events" variables, `sport_name` shows four unique running sports represented in the dataset: Outdoor Track, Indoor Track, Cross Country, and Road Race. Each of these sports are assigned a number from 1-4 according to the `sport_id` variable. From these sports, each contain a collection of events that can be run in said sport given by the `event_name` variable. There are 37 unique event types, each also associated with a number in the `event_id` variable.

```{r}
event_summary = only_run %>%
  count(sport_name, event_name, name = "count")

ggplot(event_summary, aes(x = count, y = reorder_within(event_name, count, sport_name))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  facet_wrap(~sport_name, scales = "free", ncol = 2) + 
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Running Events by Sport",
    x = "Number of Results",
    y = "Running Event"
  )
```
